Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the UniInsure Holdings Inc. Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Alex Rivera, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Alex Rivera: Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to UniInsure Holdings' Q3 2024 earnings call. Joining me on the call today are David Thompson, Chief Executive Officer; Sarah Jenkins, Chief Financial Officer; Michael Patel, Chief Underwriting Officer; and Lisa Wong, Chief Investment Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we are making today may be considered forward-looking. These statements are subject to certain risks and uncertainties that could cause our actual results to differ materially from those projected. We encourage you to review our SEC filings for a more detailed discussion of these risks and uncertainties.

I will now turn the call over to David Thompson.

David Thompson: Thank you, Alex, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. I'm pleased to report on UniInsure Holdings' performance for Q3 2024. We delivered strong results, driven by refinements in our actuarial assumptions that balanced reserve adequacy with earnings stability, an improved combined ratio reflecting disciplined underwriting across segments, proactive pricing actions that supported premium growth, manageable catastrophe losses within our risk corridor, and clear guidance pointing to continued profitability. Our focus on technical excellence in modeling and risk selection continues to yield positive outcomes, positioning us for sustainable growth.

Sarah Jenkins, our CFO, will now provide a more detailed review of our financial performance.

Sarah Jenkins: Thank you, David. Good morning, everyone. As David mentioned, we had a solid quarter. Our net income was $520 million, or $0.78 per diluted share. Key drivers of our financial performance included robust premium growth, favorable reserve developments, and steady investment returns. Our combined ratio was 92.5%, reflecting effective underwriting and claims management. Investment income for the quarter was $265 million. We continue to maintain a strong capital position, with a risk-based capital ratio of 520%, well above our target of 450% and industry peers.

Good morning again, and thanks for joining us on UniInsure Holdings' third quarter earnings call. Before we open it up to Q&A, I'd like to dive into a key driver of our results this quarter: changes in actuarial assumptions and their impacts across our book. As you know, actuarial assumptions underpin our reserve adequacy, pricing discipline, and ultimately, our earnings trajectory. In an environment shaped by persistent inflation, normalizing post-COVID mortality trends, and divergent central bank policies globally, we've made targeted updates to several key assumptions. These refinements, reviewed rigorously by our Chief Actuary and external peer reviewers in line with NAIC guidelines and emerging IFRS 17 principles, resulted in a net pre-tax charge of $285 million, or $0.42 per diluted share after tax. Let me break this down systematically.

First, on discount rates for our $180 billion long-duration liabilities, primarily life annuities and universal life products. With the Fed's terminal rate now anchored around 4.75-5.00% amid sticky core PCE inflation at 2.7%, we've increased our base discount rate by 25 basis points to 4.10% from 3.85%. This reflects updated forward curves from Bloomberg and our proprietary ALM models, incorporating the recent Treasury yield curve steepening—10-year yields up 40 bps quarter-over-quarter to 4.35%. Positively, this unlocked $420 million in reserve releases, boosting net income by $310 million after tax, as higher discounts reduce the present value of future claims. However, we remain cautious on reinvestment risk; our dynamic hedging program via interest rate swaps and Treasury futures covered 92% of this duration gap, limiting volatility to under 2% of surplus.

Contrast this with Europe, where the ECB's more dovish stance—deposits at 3.50%—prompted a 15 bps decrease in our Eurozone discount rate to 2.75%. This strengthened reserves by $110 million on our €45 billion in unit-linked and participating life policies, akin to what we've seen at peers like AXA and Allianz. In Asia-Pacific, where yields are compressing amid BOJ normalization, we held our discount steady at 2.20% but layered in scenario testing for a potential 50 bps drop, which could add $75 million to reserves next year.

Second, on mortality and morbidity assumptions, a focal point post the pandemic. Our updated 2024 experience study, blending SOA's 2023 Large Pool Mortality Table with our 15-year internal data from 2.5 million policyholders, shows credible improvements in longevity—select mortality rates down 3.2% for ages 65-80, driven by vaccines, telemedicine adoption, and delayed elective surgeries normalizing. For our $120 billion term life and whole life blocks, this necessitated a $210 million reserve strengthening, reflecting lower near-term but higher distant-horizon claims. Morbidity followed suit: disability claims frequency fell 4.5% YoY, per our Milliman collaboration, leading to a $65 million favorable adjustment in our group health and long-term care reserves.

Regionally, U.S. Medicare Advantage trends mirror UnitedHealth's reported improvements, with our PDP and MA-PD enrollment up 8% to 1.2 million lives, but we baked in a 2% morbidity uplift for obesity-related comorbidities amid GLP-1 drug shortages. In the UK, PruProtect-like products saw lapse-adjusted mortality creep up 1.8% due to heatwave impacts, partially offset by our parametric weather reinsurance treaty with Swiss Re.

Third, on policyholder behavior assumptions, including lapses, persistency, and utilization. Economic resilience—U.S. unemployment at 4.1%—drove lapses down to 5.2% annualized from 6.1%, per our behavioral models calibrated against LIMRA data. This $45 million favorable swing primarily hit our VUL and indexed UL portfolios, where anti-lapse premium flexibilities have stabilized in-force value. However, we increased utilization assumptions by 2.3% in P&C health lines, reflecting pent-up dental and behavioral health claims, adding $25 million to IBNR reserves.

Quantitatively, on our P&L and balance sheet: The net $285 million charge reduced adjusted operating income by 11% to $2.18 billion, with EPS dilution of 7%. Reserves grew 4.2% to $210 billion, maintaining a pristine 520% RBC ratio—well above our 450% target and peers like MetLife at 480%. DAC amortization accelerated by $30 million due to persistency gains, while our liability adequacy testing under LDTI passed with a 15% margin.

Strategically, these updates underscore our commitment to technical excellence. We've invested $25 million in Q3 to upgrade our Prophet and AXIS stochastic modeling platforms, enabling 10,000-scenario runs for EEV calculations and ORSA stress testing. This includes machine learning overlays for morbidity forecasting, drawing from Google Cloud partnerships similar to those at Prudential Financial. Forward-looking, our sensitivities show: +100 bps rates = $650M tailwind; -5% mortality improvement = $180M headwind. We're mitigating via excess-of-loss reinsurance on longevity (90% quota share with Hannover Re) and dynamic lapses in pricing for new biz—our Q4 book targeting 12% ROE uplift.

Regionally, U.S. P&C cat losses from Hurricane Helene shaved 1.5 points off combined ratio to 92.3%, but assumption discipline here is stable. In Japan, super-longevity trends mirror Sumitomo Life's challenges, prompting a JGAAP-to-IFRS 17 bridge with 20% CSM volatility hedge.

In summary, these assumption changes reflect disciplined, data-driven stewardship—not one-offs, but evolutions in a volatile world. They position UniInsure for sustainable 10-12% EPS growth into 2025, with ROE expansion to 14%.

Now, let's dive deeper into our combined ratio performance for the quarter, both overall and by segment. As you know, the combined ratio remains our north star metric for underwriting discipline in Property & Casualty, calculated as the sum of our loss and loss adjustment expense ratio—LLAE—and our underwriting expense ratio, or UEX. A combined ratio below 100% generates underwriting income, and we're proud to say we've delivered eight straight quarters under 100%, underscoring the strength of our pricing, risk selection, and operational efficiencies.

For Q3, our overall P&C combined ratio came in at 91.8%, a 140 basis point improvement from 93.2% in Q3 last year and 30 basis points better than our Q2 this year at 92.1%. This drove $450 million in underwriting income for the quarter, up 25% year-over-year. Excluding catastrophes—which totaled $220 million pre-tax, or 2.8 points on the ratio, primarily from California wildfires and Midwest thunderstorms—the accident year ex-cat combined ratio was an exceptional 89.0%, down 180 basis points from prior year.

Breaking it down: Loss Ratio at 63.4%, down 120 basis points year-over-year. Favorable drivers included a 4% decline in auto physical damage severity due to stabilizing supply chain issues on parts, and 2 points of favorable prior year development, mainly in workers' comp from better-than-expected claim closures. Frequency remained stable at 98% of baseline in personal lines.

Expense Ratio: 28.4%, a 20 basis point improvement, reflecting our multi-year UEX modernization program. Key wins here: commission reductions from straight-through processing now at 85% in personal auto quotes, and a 15% cut in variable acquisition costs via our partnership with Guidewire's digital platform.

For the first three quarters, the overall combined ratio is 92.0%, positioning us well against our full-year guidance of 91-93%. This compares favorably to the industry average of 96.5% per ISO data, and even outperforms peers like Progressive at 93.2% and Travelers at 94.1% in their latest quarters.

Segment breakdown: Personal Lines, 57% of P&C premiums, combined ratio of 90.5%, our best Q3 since 2019. Auto: 92.1%, down 200 bps YoY. Loss ratio improved to 64.2% on lower bodily injury frequency—now trending 3% below pre-pandemic levels—partly due to our ApexDrive telematics program, which now covers 2.8 million policies and discounts 1.1 million safe drivers by an average 22%. We've also hiked rates 9.2% in non-California states, with retention steady at 87%. California remains challenged at 98.4% due to Prop 103 rate suppression and wildfire cats, but our exit from high-risk ZIPs has stemmed the bleed. Homeowners/Dwellings: 87.2%, stellar performance. Loss ratio at 58.1%, benefiting from 5% lower weather-related severity after a mild hurricane season start. Our smart home IoT integrations—partnered with Hippo and Lemonade tech stacks—have reduced claims by 12% in pilot states like Texas and Florida. Expense ratio here ticked down to 29.1% on digital underwriting efficiencies.

Commercial Lines, 32% of P&C premiums, combined ratio of 93.2%, up slightly from 92.8% YoY due to one-off large losses, but ex-cat it's 90.5%. Small Commercial under $50k premium: 91.0%. Loss ratio 65.8%, pressured by 6% inflation in construction repairs, but offset by 11% rate increases and our AI-powered risk scoring model, which improved loss ratio pick-up by 150 bps. Middle Market and Excess & Surplus (E&S): 95.1%, reflecting $85 million in cat losses from Texas hailstorms. E&S continues to shine with a 88.4% ex-cat ratio, fueled by 15% rate momentum in a hardening market—think layers above $10 million where capacity is tight post-2023 losses at peers like Chubb. We've grown E&S premiums 22% YoY by leaning into cyber and D&O amid rising SEC climate disclosures.

Specialty and International, 11% of P&C premiums, combined ratio of 89.7%, our profit engine. Domestic Specialty like marine and agribusiness: 87.5%, with loss ratio at 60.2% on benign marine claims and our drone-based crop underwriting cutting ag severity 8%. International: 91.4%, flat YoY. Europe improved to 90.2% on UK motor rate hikes post-Flood Re expansions, while Asia-Pacific ticked up to 93.1% from Thailand floods, but our reinsurance tower—95% quota share above $50 million—capped net exposure.

Year-to-date trends are encouraging: Auto frequency is normalizing post-COVID driving surges, with our GLMs now incorporating real-time inflation data from Verisk. Cat losses are tracking 10% below our 1-in-50 year plan at $410 million, thanks to robust modeling from RMS 20 platform. However, social inflation remains a tailwind risk—up 4% in litigated claims—prompting us to bolster defense counsel networks and pursue more subrogation via Chain That software.

Regionally: U.S., 82% of premiums, Southeast combined ratio at 94.2% due to Florida hurricane prep costs, but we've non-renewed 15% of coastal exposure, mirroring Allstate's strategy. Midwest ag is a bright spot at 88.5%. Europe, 10%: 91.0%, aided by Motor Insurance Database efficiencies under Solvency II. Asia/LatAm, 8%: 92.8%, with growth in India micro-insurance despite monsoons.

Operationally, our $250 million tech investment is paying off: Generative AI for claims triage has slashed cycle times 28% to under 14 days, directly supporting expense leverage. We're also rolling out climate-resilient pricing via proprietary cat models, stress-testing for 1-in-200 year events like Ian-scale hurricanes.

Strategically, we're optimizing the portfolio—targeting 60/40 personal/commercial mix by 2025—while pursuing 8-10% earned rate adequacy. Reinsurance renewal in January locked in 5% cheaper terms on our $1.2 billion tower, with aggregate covers extended to absorb social inflation. Looking ahead, we see tailwinds from potential ILR issuance and partnerships like our Allianz Re cat bond for wildfire layers.

As we wrap up this solid quarter with a combined ratio of 96.5%—our best third-quarter result since 2019—I'm pleased to provide our forward-looking guidance on this key metric. For those new to our story, the combined ratio remains the north star for our property and casualty underwriting discipline: losses and loss adjustment expenses plus other underwriting expenses, divided by earned premiums. Below 100% means we're generating underwriting profit to fuel our investments and returns.

Q3's 96.5% CR benefited from 4 points of favorable prior-year reserve development, primarily in our commercial auto book, and a 2-point cat tailwind as Hurricane Helene's impacts came in lighter than our initial models at just $150 million pre-tax. Ex-cats, our underlying loss ratio held steady at 62%, reflecting our aggressive rate actions—up 8.2% year-over-year across personal lines—and tighter underwriting guidelines on high-hazard risks like coastal property.

For Q4 2024, we're guiding to a combined ratio of 94% to 96%, implying a sequential improvement of 50 to 250 basis points. This assumes normalized catastrophe activity—around $200 million pre-tax, or roughly 1.5 points—aligned with RMS modeling for the back half of fire season in California and potential winter storms in the Northeast.

Loss Ratio Dynamics expected at 61-63%: We anticipate a 100-basis-point improvement from embedded pricing gains, now flowing through at 9% in personal auto and 12% in homeowners. Bodily injury severity remains a watch item, up 6% YoY due to litigation trends and social inflation, but our telematics program—now penetrating 45% of our auto policies via our ApexDrive app—has delivered a 15% reduction in claim frequency for safe drivers. In commercial multi-peril, we're seeing stabilization post-supply chain disruptions, with repair costs moderating as OEM parts availability improves.

Expense Ratio expected at 32-33%: We'll hold this flat to slightly down, thanks to our 'Tech 25' initiative: a $250 million multi-year investment in AI-driven underwriting and claims automation. We've already cut cycle times by 25% in auto claims using computer vision for damage assessment, partnering with CCC Intelligent Solutions, and our robotic process automation has shaved 1.5 points off the expense ratio YTD. Headcount optimization—down 3% via attrition—combined with vendor consolidation, keeps us lean.

Regionally, U.S. operations, 85% of premiums, should drive the midpoint at 93%, buoyed by Midwest and Southeast growth. Europe, at 10% of mix, faces headwinds from UK motor claims inflation up 7% on medicals, capping us at 97%, while Asia-Pacific's commercial lines expansion in Singapore and Australia supports 92%.

Full-Year 2024 Guidance: 95-96%, with a midpoint of 95.2%—200 basis points ahead of consensus. This reflects $450 million in total cat losses YTD, below our original $600 million plan, and premium growth of 7.5% to $28.5 billion. Ex-cats and PYD, underlying CR is 94.8%, underscoring our rate adequacy.

For 2025 Full-Year Guidance: 93-95%, a 200-basis-point improvement at the midpoint. This assumes mid-single-digit earned premium growth to $30 billion, with cats at $500 million, 1.5-2% of premiums, per Verisk cat aggregator models.

Key drivers: Pricing and Portfolio Actions—we'll file for 6-8% increases in homeowners and 4-6% in auto, targeting ROE expansion to 12% in personal lines. We're pruning $400 million in underperforming small commercial risks, shifting to higher-attachment excess & surplus layers where margins exceed 25%.

Cat and Risk Mitigation: Enhanced climate modeling via RMS v18 has improved wind deductibles uptake to 60% in Florida, reducing net exposure. Reinsurance renewal in January locks in 20% cheaper terms on our $2 billion tower, thanks to diversified capacity from Swiss Re and RenaissanceRe.

Expense Leverage: 'Tech 25' scales up, targeting 30.5% expense ratio via generative AI for fraud detection—already flagging 20% more suspicious claims—and cloud migration saving $50 million annually. We're expanding ApexDrive to homeowners with IoT sensors from Google Nest, aiming for 10% frequency reduction.

Strategic tailwinds include a softening auto rate environment post-2023 peaks, but hardening property amid wildfires. Regulatory tailwinds like Florida's post-Surfside reforms support disciplined growth, while challenges like OSHA's proposed crane regulations could pressure construction liability—we've stress-tested for 5% severity uptick.

Risks to the guide include a 10% cat exceedance pushing CR to 97% or persistent social inflation, but our 35% statutory capital buffer and $1.2 billion liquidity position us resiliently. We're committed to 10-12% ROE through the cycle, with P&C delivering 95% average CR.

Before we open the floor to questions, I'd like to dive deeper into one of the key drivers behind our premium volume performance this quarter: the impact of our disciplined pricing actions across our Property & Casualty and Specialty lines. As you know, we've been navigating a dynamic market environment characterized by persistent claims inflation—running at 10-12% in auto physical damage and 8-9% in workers' comp—coupled with elevated catastrophe activity, including the ripple effects from Hurricane Beryl and the California wildfires earlier this year. Our pricing strategy has been pivotal in delivering 7.2% year-over-year gross written premium growth to $14.8 billion for the quarter, outpacing the industry average of 5.1% as reported by AM Best.

Overall, we implemented average rate increases of 8.5% across our book, weighted by premium volume. This was a step-up from the 7.2% we achieved in Q2, reflecting our data-driven approach to recapturing margins amid a loss ratio that improved 210 basis points to 92.4%. The net effect? Premium volume elasticity played out favorably: while policy count growth softened to +1.8% from +3.5% in the prior year—due to some price-sensitive attrition in personal auto—our per-policy premium uplift more than compensated, driving net earned premium expansion of 6.9% to $13.2 billion.

Segment-wise, Personal Lines, 55% of our GWP: auto pricing rose 9.8% on average, with comprehensive and collision lines seeing the biggest hikes at 11.2% to address repair cost inflation tied to supply chain disruptions in OEM parts. Homeowners' rates increased 7.6%, moderated in non-cat-prone states like the Midwest. This translated to a 5.4% premium volume increase to $8.1 billion, despite a 1.2% dip in auto policies in force, as retention held steady at 87.2%—bolstered by our ApexDrive telematics program, which now covers 2.4 million policies and delivers 15% better loss picks through real-time driving data. Comparatively, peers like Progressive reported similar auto retention pressures but lower rate discipline, resulting in flatter volume growth.

Commercial Lines—40% of GWP—we executed 8.1% rate adequacy improvements, with middle-market packages up 9.3% and excess & surplus lines at 10.7%, capitalizing on hardening market dynamics post-2023's $100 billion+ industry cat losses. Premium volume here surged 9.1% to $5.9 billion, fueled by 4.2% new business growth and 89.5% renewal retention. Our technical edge came from deploying GLMs enhanced with machine learning via our partnership with Einstein Analytics, which segmented risks down to ZIP-code granularity, yielding a 12% improvement in pricing accuracy and reducing adverse selection by 3 points.

Regionally, in the U.S., 72% of our book, East Coast pricing averaged 9.2% amid secondary perils like severe convective storms, driving 8.1% volume growth but with California homeowners' rates capped at 6.8% due to regulatory scrutiny from the DOI—similar to challenges faced by State Farm and Allstate. Europe, 15% of GWP, saw more modest 6.4% increases under Solvency II constraints, yet delivered 4.7% volume uplift in UK motor and D&O, aided by our Brexit-adjusted reinsurance towers. Asia-Pacific, our growth engine at 13%, benefited from 11.2% hikes in Australian commercial amid flood reinsurance repricing, pushing volume up 12.4%—outpacing regional peers like IAG.

Strategically, these pricing changes underscore our 'Profitable Growth 2.0' framework: we're not chasing top-line at the expense of returns. Our earned ROE guidance remains 12-14% for FY24, supported by a 96.8% combined ratio—down 140 bps YoY—thanks to pricing outpacing loss trends by 150 bps. We've also layered in non-rate levers like 5% dividend relief from our quota-share reinsurance with Swiss Re, freeing $450 million in capital for selective expansion into high-margin E&S. Looking forward, we anticipate market softening in auto by mid-2025 as inflation moderates, but our advanced analytics—now incorporating climate risk modeling from RMS v17—position us to maintain 7-9% earned pricing gains. Elasticity tests show that for every 1% rate hike, we see only 0.3% policy attrition in personal lines, validating our approach.

Finally, I'd like to spend a few minutes on total catastrophe losses impact, one of the most critical line items for our industry. Cats represent the tail risk that can swing our earnings quarter to quarter, and they've been front and center this year amid an active hurricane season and persistent wildfire activity. I'll break this down in USD terms, as a percentage of gross written premium—or GWP—and provide some color on trends, regional drivers, our mitigation strategies, and forward guidance.

For Q3 2024, our total catastrophe losses, net of reinsurance and reinstatement premiums, came in at $1.2 billion. That's up 45% from $825 million in Q3 2023, but down 15% sequentially from Q2's $1.4 billion peak. As a percentage of GWP, this equates to 4.2%—elevated versus our three-year average of 2.8%, but within our targeted cat corridor of 3-5% for property lines.

Year-to-date through Q3, cumulative net cat losses stand at $3.1 billion, or 3.5% of YTD GWP of $89 billion. This compares to $2.4 billion, or 2.9% of GWP, in the prior-year period. The step-up reflects a busier-than-normal North Atlantic hurricane season, with events like Hurricane Helene and Milton contributing roughly 60% of our Q3 cat book; and secondary perils like California wildfires and European convective storms adding another 25%. For context, the global PCS index for North America was up 30% YoY in Q3, aligning with our experience.

Regional and peril breakdown: U.S. Property Portfolio, 65% of total cats: $780 million, or 6.1% of segment GWP. Helene alone generated $450 million in net losses on our homeowners and commercial multi-peril books, exacerbated by storm surge claims in Florida and the Carolinas. Wildfires in the Pacific Northwest added $150 million, driven by our E&S lines exposure in high-hazard zones. Our U.S. cat load was 180 basis points above our actuarial expectations, per our RMS v18 models.

Europe & Bermuda, 20%: $240 million, or 3.2% of GWP. Flooding from Storm Boris in Central Europe hit our motor and SME property renewals hard, with $120 million in attributed losses. We've seen favorable development here, clawing back $30 million from prior IBNR reserves.

Asia-Pacific & Rest of World, 15%: $180 million, primarily from Typhoon Yagi in Southeast Asia, impacting our reinsurance quota shares and direct crop insurance in Vietnam and the Philippines.

Excluding cats, our attritional loss ratio held steady at 58%, keeping the underlying combined operating ratio—or COR—at 92.5%, a testament to our pricing discipline. However, the elevated cat load pushed our all-in COR to 102.8% for Q3, diluting EPS by about $0.45 per share.

On our technical initiatives and strategic response: Reinsurance optimization—our 2024 program, renewed January 1st at a 12% lower cost than 2023 thanks to our strong balance sheet (A.M. Best A+ rating), features a $2.5 billion all-peril tower with Swiss Re and Munich Re layers. We layered in excess-of-loss covers at $500 million XS $500 million for U.S. windstorm, capturing 75% cession rates on peak perils. Reinstatement premiums added $150 million to the P&L this quarter, partially offsetting gross losses.

Advanced cat modeling and portfolio actions: We've integrated AI-driven enhancements into our proprietary cat platform, partnering with Karen Clark & Company for ensemble modeling that fuses RMS, AIR, and our internal climate-adjusted scenarios. This allowed us to non-renew $400 million in GWP from high-cat U.S. Gulf Coast exposures post-2023 Ida retrospectives, reducing our modeled 1-in-100 APV by 8%. We're also piloting parametric triggers with reinsurers like RenaissanceRe for faster wildfire payouts, targeting sub-7-day settlements.

Regionally, in California, we're de-risking via higher deductibles on FAIR Plan alternatives and pushing mitigation credits—up to 15% premium discounts—for clients adopting wildfire-resistant retrofits, akin to Allstate's successful Glide Path program. In Europe, we're embedding NatCat aggregation limits into our industrial property wordings to cap flood accumulations.

Strategically, this underscores our focus on climate-resilient underwriting. With IPCC AR6 projections showing a 20-30% uptick in TC intensity by 2030, we're guiding for cat losses of 3.0-3.5% of GWP in FY2024, assuming no top-end events like a Cat 5 landfall. For 2025 renewals, we anticipate 8-10% rate adequacy across P&C lines, with cat-heavy books seeing 12-15%, mirroring industry trends from recent Verisk analytics.

In summary, while Q3 cats were punishing, our diversified book, robust reinsurance, and tech-forward risk management position us well. Ex-cats, the business is firing on all cylinders.

Michael Patel: Thank you, Sarah. I'd like to provide an update on our underwriting performance. We've seen continued strong performance in our commercial lines segment. We are actively managing our exposure to catastrophe-prone regions like the Southeast U.S. and have implemented several initiatives to improve our risk selection, including enhanced telematics adoption and AI-driven portfolio optimization, which directly support the combined ratio improvements Sarah outlined.

Operator, we are now ready to open the line for questions.

Operator: Thank you. [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from Emily Carter with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Emily Carter: Good morning. Can you provide more color on the changes in actuarial assumptions and their ongoing impact?

Sarah Jenkins: Good morning, Emily. As I detailed earlier, the net $285 million pre-tax charge from those updates primarily stemmed from mortality improvements requiring reserve strengthening and policyholder behavior shifts. The discount rate hikes provided a tailwind, but we're hedged against volatility. These are data-driven evolutions, and our sensitivities indicate resilience—positioning us for 10-12% EPS growth ahead.

Operator: Our next question comes from Robert Kline with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Robert Kline: Good morning. Could you discuss the impact of catastrophe losses on your business this quarter?

David Thompson: Good morning, Robert. The $1.2 billion net cat hit was within our corridor at 4.2% of GWP, driven by Helene and wildfires. Our reinsurance tower and non-renewals mitigated the worst, keeping underlying COR at 92.5%. We're guiding 3-3.5% for the full year, with enhanced modeling for 2025.

Operator: Our next question comes from Lisa Patel with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Lisa Patel: What is the expected impact of pricing changes on premium volume going forward?

Sarah Jenkins: Thanks, Lisa. Our 8.5% average hikes drove 7.2% GWP growth this quarter, with elasticity favorable at 0.3% attrition per 1% increase. We're targeting 7-9% earned gains into 2025, balancing volume and ROE at 12-14%, supported by analytics and reinsurance relief.

Operator: Our next question comes from Tom Reilly with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Tom Reilly: Can you elaborate on combined ratio guidance for next year?

Sarah Jenkins: Absolutely, Tom. 93-95% for 2025 midpoint, driven by pricing, tech efficiencies from Tech 25, and cat mitigation. Ex-cats underlying at low 90s, with ROE to 12%. Risks like social inflation are stress-tested.

Operator: [No further questions at this time.]

David Thompson: Thank you for your questions and your interest in UniInsure Holdings. In closing, we are confident in our ability to continue delivering strong results and creating value for our shareholders. Thank you for joining us today.

Operator: This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.
